title: Harbor and Regiment
premise: In the waning months of a long war, battlefield nurse Hazel Blackwood keeps a secret ledger of soldiers whose names officers have struck from official records, believing that every erased person deserves to be remembered. When an injured child is abandoned at her field hospital's door with orders to forget his face, Hazel recognizes the boy as the son of Captain Elias Vane — the man who once saved her life and is now officially declared an enemy collaborator. Torn between regimental loyalty and the truth in her ledger, Hazel smuggles the child toward safety while uncovering that Vane was silenced because he knew which officers had been selling their own men's positions. As armistice negotiations stall and the conspirators close in, Hazel must choose between burning her ledger to protect her found family of nurses and orderlies or producing it as testimony. In the end she testifies, Vane is cleared posthumously after dying protecting the boy, and Hazel finds belonging not in a nation or a regiment but in the small household of survivors who carry each other's names forward.
about_author: A. M. Hartwell is the pen name of a former military archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from forgotten wars. They write historical fiction about the people official records leave behind.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Hazel Blackwood, POV. In a muddy field hospital near the front, Hazel records the name of a dead private omitted from the morning report, hiding the ledger beneath a floorboard. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: she has done this for twelve years, and the war's end feels both imminent and impossibly far.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. During a bombardment, an orderly finds a wounded boy of about eight left at the hospital entrance with a note: forget this face. Hazel recognizes the handwriting instantly — it belongs to Captain Elias Vane, the man who pulled her from a burning aid station years ago. The beat is dread wrapped in tenderness.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Silences
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Hazel's POV. Through interwoven memory we learn how Vane saved her, how they made a peacetime promise that if either ever needed the other, no rank or flag would stand in the way. The beat is bittersweet nostalgia sharpening into resolve: the promise has come due.

chapters.title: Declared Enemy
chapters.summary: Sergeant Imogen Pryce, POV. Official word arrives that Captain Vane has defected and is wanted for treason; all correspondence with him is forbidden. Pryce, Hazel's closest friend and a rule-keeper to her bones, notices Hazel's reaction and says nothing — yet. The beat is loyalty beginning to strain.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Would Not Speak
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. The child, Tomas, refuses to speak but draws obsessively: a map, a bridge, a man's face. Hazel realizes he may have seen something worth killing over. She hides his drawings inside the ledger. The beat is protective ferocity hardening into conspiracy.

chapters.title: Colonel Ashworth's Inspection
chapters.summary: Pryce, POV. Colonel Ashworth tours the hospital asking pointed questions about unauthorized personnel and missing paperwork. He lingers at Hazel's ward a moment too long. Pryce covers for her friend without knowing why, and hates herself for it. The beat is complicity born of love.

chapters.title: What the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Cross-referencing her ledger with supply manifests, Hazel discovers a pattern: men who died in 'friendly fire' incidents all served under officers now promoted and decorated. Vane wasn't a traitor — he found the same pattern. The beat is revelation and rising fear.

chapters.title: The Orderly Who Knew Too Much
chapters.summary: Orderly Finn Calloway, POV. Finn, who found the boy, is caught copying one of Tomas's drawings and is arrested on fabricated charges of theft. His arrest is a message: someone knows the child is here. The beat is guilt and the first true cost of sheltering Tomas.

chapters.title: A Promise in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. A half-starved deserter delivers a coded message from Vane: bring the boy to the mill bridge before the armistice is signed, or not at all. Hazel must decide within days. Pryce catches her packing and finally demands the truth. The beat is the promise laid bare between friends.

chapters.title: The Quarrel
chapters.summary: Pryce, POV. Pryce and Hazel fight bitterly: Pryce argues the ledger and the boy will destroy everyone in the hospital; Hazel argues silence is how the guilty stay decorated. Pryce walks out — then quietly leaves the hospital's ambulance keys on Hazel's cot. The beat is loyalty choosing a side without admitting it.

chapters.title: Roads Behind the Lines
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Hazel and Tomas travel by night through shattered countryside, posing as refugees. Tomas finally speaks, telling her his father made him memorize names — the same kind of names in her ledger. The beat is fragile trust blooming between two people built from omissions.

chapters.title: The Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV (child's-eye). At a checkpoint, a young soldier nearly discovers them; Tomas lies for the first time in his life, calling Hazel his mother. The lie works, and something in Hazel breaks open hearing it. The beat is found family crystallizing in a single improvised word.

chapters.title: Ashworth Closes In
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth, POV. Ashworth interrogates Finn and pieces together Hazel's flight. We see his motive: the armistice will bring tribunals, and the ledger of omitted names would hang him and his circle. He orders the bridge watched. The beat is cold, bureaucratic menace.

chapters.title: The Mill Bridge
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. At the ruined mill, Hazel waits with Tomas through a freezing night. Vane appears — gaunt, hunted, alive. Their reunion is clipped by danger, but the old promise holds. He explains what he knows and why the boy matters more than either of them. The beat is relief shadowed by doom.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Crossing
chapters.summary: Vane, POV. Ashworth's men spring the trap. Vane holds the crossing so Hazel and Tomas can escape through the marshes, taking a fatal wound in the process. His last words ask Hazel not to save his name — save the others'. The beat is sacrifice fulfilling the promise at last.

chapters.title: Burn It or Bear It
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Hiding in a bombed chapel, Hazel faces the choice: burn the ledger so no one else dies for it, or carry it to the armistice commission as testimony. Tomas takes her hand and recites his father's list from memory — the ledger exists in him now too. The beat is grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Armistice That Isn't
chapters.summary: Pryce, POV. Back at the hospital, rumors swirl that the signing has stalled — Ashworth's faction is delaying until loose ends are cut. Pryce realizes Hazel will be next. She steals the colonel's own dispatches proving the friendly-fire cover-up and goes after Hazel. The beat is loyalty finally overtaking obedience.

chapters.title: Reunion of the Forgotten
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Pryce finds Hazel and Tomas; Finn escapes custody and joins them with two other orderlies. In a farmhouse cellar, the found family assembles around the ledger, each adding names they've carried silently for years. The beat is belonging discovered not in blood or nation but in shared witness.

chapters.title: The Tribunal at Dawn
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided together. As the armistice is finally signed, Hazel stands before the commission with the ledger, Tomas's testimony, and Pryce's stolen dispatches. Ashworth's defense collapses when his own signature appears beside an omitted name. The beat is terror becoming triumph, quiet and costly.

chapters.title: What Names Cost
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Ashworth is arrested; Finn is exonerated; Vane is posthumously cleared. But Hazel learns some names in her ledger belong to men who did terrible things, and remembering them is harder than she imagined. The beat is the moral weight of truth — loyalty to facts over comfort.

chapters.title: The House by the Harbor
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Months later, the group settles in a coastal harbor town where Hazel opens a small convalescent home. Tomas, adopted informally by all of them, adds the final entry to the ledger: his father's full name, restored. The beat is healing without forgetting.

chapters.title: Harbor and Regiment
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. On the anniversary of the armistice, Hazel reads the ledger aloud at the harbor as the regimental band plays in town — the institution and the individuals, side by side at last. She closes the book, not because the silences are over, but because now they are shared. The beat is peace earned, imperfect and permanent.
